terms.grammar: noun, second declension, neuter; no plural in classical use
evidence: Traupman 66: vīrus percrēbrēscit, there is a virus going around
terms.comment: The modern sense, taken by the sciences from Latin. Classically vīrus is slime, venom, poison, and a stench (Verg. G. 1.129, Lewis & Short); eighteenth-century doctors used it of the matter that carried smallpox (Morgan–Owens). Of a computer virus, the same word.
Morgan–Owens’s tentative paraphrase, beside morbus vīrōsus and pathogonum; vīrōsus is classically slimy or foul-smelling.

phrases.english: there is a virus going around

sources: Lewis & Short: virus · Lewis & Short: virosus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 66, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. virus.
